title: Days for everyone
hook: Eid is for the poor, the orphan, the traveler too

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eid al-Adha: first the prayer, then the sacrifice, then the meat carried out the door. Your line was share the feast. Whose hands did your plate end up in? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-six.

Al-Bukhari keeps a sharp little saying, reported from Abu Hurayrah. In paraphrase: the worst food is the food of a wedding feast where the rich are invited and the poor are left out. The worst food. Not spoiled food, not stolen food. A good meal, at a happy party, with the wrong guest list. The saying is about a wedding. Some readers hear it about any feast, the two Eids included. So on the last day of this stretch of the festival year, a question about the guest list: who is Eid for?
screen: `THE WORST FOOD.` → `THE WRONG GUEST LIST.` → `WHO IS EID FOR?`

segments.voice: Look at how the two Eids are built, and the guest list is written into them. Before Eid al-Fitr, there's zakat al-fitr, the charity of the fast's end. Ibn 'Abbas reports in Sunan Abi Dawud that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, made it a purification for the one who fasted, and food for the poor, and that it counts as zakat when it's paid before the prayer. Some read that timing as a way to make sure the poor eat on the feast day too. At Eid al-Adha, as yesterday, the meat of the sacrifice leaves the house by design. Second, the orphan. Surah al-Insan praises people who, in Pickthall's words, "feed with food the needy wretch, the orphan and the prisoner, for love of Him." A day of new clothes is a hard day for a child with no one to buy them. Some communities make a point of new clothes and gifts for orphans before Eid. Third, the traveler. The Qur'an names the wayfarer, the person far from home, among those owed kindness. On a feast day, that's the student who couldn't fly home, the new arrival, the night-shift worker. And now the whole stretch we've walked. The sacred months. Muharram and Ashura. Rabi' al-Awwal. Rajab and Sha'ban getting ready. Ramadan planned, kept with family, kept at the mosque, finished in the last ten. Eid al-Fitr and its new road home. Dhul Qa'dah's packing, Dhul Hijjah at home, and the feast of the sacrifice. A whole year of days. And each one, at its best, with room at the table.
screen: `FOOD FOR THE POOR BEFORE THE PRAYER.` · `THE ORPHAN AT THE FEAST.` · `THE TRAVELER FAR FROM HOME.` · `A YEAR OF DAYS, ROOM AT THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: The practice: invite someone alone. Settle, and breathe. Go slowly through the people you know: at work, on your street, in your family, at school, at a mosque or a club. Look for the one who's likely to spend the next holiday by themselves. A widowed neighbor. A colleague a long way from home. A student. Let one face come and stay. Then picture the invitation: a meal, a coffee, a walk. Simple words, nothing grand. If you pray, you can remember them by name. If you don't, just hold the picture of the empty chair filled. The bell holds the time.
Days for everyone. The festival year built so that the poor eat, the orphan is dressed and the traveler is fed on the feast day too. Today's word.

Your line: no one alone on eid. Today, send the invitation, or set the date for the next feast day. Tomorrow a new stretch begins, on Islam in the world today: many ways of being Muslim. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Before the Eid al-Fitr prayer, Muslims pay zakat al-fitr so that people in need can eat on the feast day, and at Eid al-Adha the meat of the sacrifice is shared with the poor; mosques and families often open their Eid meals to people who are alone, far from home or in need.

fork.setup: you're planning a big Eid meal. the guest list is full of family and friends who can host you back. what does the saying in al-Bukhari warn against?
options: a feast where the rich are invited and the poor are left out.
fork.reveal: it calls that the worst food: a good meal, at a happy party, with the wrong guest list.

original.note: Arabic: the Qur'an's phrase for the wayfarer, the traveler far from home.

trapdoor: what you thought: Eid is a family holiday.
what it means: a feast built with a guest list: the poor fed before the prayer, the sacrifice shared, the orphan and the traveler remembered.
what a scholar hears: zakat al-fitr in Abu Dawud, al-Hajj 22:36, al-Insan 76:8, and the warning about the feast that leaves out the poor in al-Bukhari.

notes: Bukhari 5177 is reported from Abu Hurayrah, partly as his own words in some chains (also Muslim 1432 as the Prophet's saying); the script says 'reported from Abu Hurayrah'. Confirm the framing.

'The Qur'an lists the wayfarer... again and again': the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil) appears in several verses (e.g., 2:177, 2:215, 9:60); the script says only that the Qur'an names the wayfarer among those owed kindness.
'Some communities make a point of new clothes and gifts for orphans before Eid' is a description of custom without a source; confirm.
Block-end look-back names days 1353–1365 from the index titles; days 1357–1361 were written by another agent.
Original: ابن السبيل is 'son of the road'; the note avoids the literal etymology under the claims rule.

Editor: the hook no longer stretches the wedding-feast saying into 'a warning about every celebration' (now 'some readers hear it about any feast'); zakat al-fitr now follows Abu Dawud 1609 (counts as zakat before the prayer) with the feeding purpose framed as a reading; shortened the repeat of yesterday's 22:36 line and replaced the myth item that duplicated day 1365's.
